__NOTOC__

NEX is Nintendo's networking library for game servers. All first party online 3DS and Wii U titles use NEX. 3rd party developers could also use NEX for their 3DS and Wii U games if they wished. Nintendo continued to use NEX into the Nintendo Switch era, however it was replaced with [[Online/Nintendo_Switch_Online/NPLN|NPLN]] in 2021. See [[Online/Nintendo_Switch_Online/NEX|NEX (NSO)]] for details on the Nintendo Switch's implementation of NEX.

NEX was not made from scratch by Nintendo. It is based on [http://web.archive.org/web/20180823162719/http://quazal.com/rendez-vous.htm Quazal Rendez-Vous] (also seen as '''RDV'''). Nintendo licensed Rendez-Vous and, over time, made their own modifications/extensions to the libraries to fit their own needs. Since anyone could license a copy of Rendez-Vous from Quazal, however, many concepts seen in NEX can also been seen in other non-Nintendo titles and on non-Nintendo platforms, such as games made by Ubisoft (who bought Quazal in 2010), Test Drive Unlimited on the PlayStation 2, etc. An incomplete list of games which use Rendez-Vous can be found at https://www.mobygames.com/group/8210/middleware-rendez-vous.

== Transport ==

NEX uses UDP with a custom reliability layer called [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/PRUDP|PRUDP]]. The connection to the server uses similar (and at times, the same) concepts as what is used to connect to other players via p2p, and each connection uses a version of [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/Kerberos|kerberos]] where the target user is the game server.

== Service Protocols ==

Once a client has established a [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/PRUDP|PRUDP]] connection to the server, each end of the connection may begin sending messages to each other. These messages encode the target [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/Protocols|service protocol]], target protocol method, and method parameters/response values.

== Servers ==

There are always at least 2 servers used by NEX, the ''authentication server'' and the ''secure server''. The client first connects to the ''authentication server'' and attempts to login to the clients game server account.

'''Note:''' ''The users game server account is NOT the same as their network account. See below for details.''

The ''authentication server'' only has a single protocol, the [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/Protocols/TicketGranting|TicketGranting]] protocol. After passing authentication, the ''authentication server'' sends the client the address of the ''secure server'' as well as a connection ticket. The client then disconnects from the ''authentication server'' and connects to the ''secure server'' with the ticket. The ''secure server'' is where the games actual protocols live.

Optionally, the ''authentication server'' may also send the client the address of a ''special server'', and a list of protocol IDs which belong to said server. If used, the client connects to both the main ''secure server'' and the ''special server'', and any requests sent for "special" protocols are directed to the ''special server'' instead. For example, a game could put matchmaking on the ''secure server'' and leaderboards on the ''special server'' in order to not split server resources between protocols. Nintendo never used the ''special server''.

== Accounts ==

Since Nintendo did not make NEX from scratch, they had to integrate certain Rendez-Vous concepts into their own servers. One of these concepts being accounts. Rendez-Vous ships with, and is designed to use, it's own integrated account system. Rendez-Vous was also designed before the concept of multi-server game networks existed, so each server is designed to be entirely self contained. To get around this, Nintendo creates game server accounts when registering for network accounts, ties these game server accounts to the network account, and then syncs the newly created game server account to all game servers on the network. This means that, technically, on Nintendo Network you have a single dedicated account on every game server that exists in the network, which Nintendo keeps in sync. This also means that, by using the [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/Protocols/AccountManagement|AccountManagement]] protocol, you can login with your own game server account and create a new game server account on that game server. This account would not be tied to a network account, and may or may not be synced properly to other games in the network.

Each game server account has the following core parts:

{| class="wikitable"
! Name !! Description
|-
| PID || An internal ID representing an account. On Nintendo Network these are always a uint32, and are assigned sequentially counting down from 1800000000. This value is the same as the users Nintendo Network ID PID. For example, the Nintendo Network ID <code>prodtest1</code> has the PID 1799999999.
|-
| Username || The game server accounts username. In regualr Rendez-Vous this would be a normal username, usually set by the user. On Nintendo Network, Nintendo automatically assigns the username to be the string representation of the account PID. For example, the Nintendo Network ID <code>prodtest1</code> has the game server username <code>"1799999999"</code>.
|-
| Password || The game server accounts password. In regualr Rendez-Vous this would be a normal password, usually set by the user. On Nintendo Network, Nintendo automatically assigns the password to be a random 16 character string.
|-
| Email || The game server accounts email address. In regualr Rendez-Vous this would be a normal email address, usually set by the user. On Nintendo Network, this is never used.
|-
| Group || The group the game server account belongs to. The exact use of groups is not known, but is likely tied to account permissions. All game server accounts on Nintendo Network are assigned the group ID <code>0x20</code>.
|-
| Extra data || Any additional data tied to the account. There are several methods available to create accounts, including Nintendo-specific methods, which all take in different data.
|}

The accounts password is typically not sent to the game server directly after creating the account. Instead, it is used to generate the users connection ticket. See [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/Kerberos|Kerberos]] for more details on connection tickets. Since the password is used to create and validate the connection ticket, this means that the password does not need to be sent over the wire to login.

There are also a number of special accounts. These are used mostly for internal processes, besides the <code>guest</code> account which is available for all users. The special accounts available, and their uses, may differ between Rendez-Vous-based titles. Based on the gaps in accounts, and by the ranges where other games have their own special accounts, PIDs 1-99 are likely reserved for Rendez-Vous specifically, whereas PIDs 100+ are available for developer use.

The following special accounts exist on Nintendo Network:

! PID !! Username !! Description !! Password

|-
| 2 || <code>Quazal Rendez-Vous</code> || Represents the ''secure server''. This is target user in [[{{FULLPAGENAME}}/Kerberos|kerberos]] ||
|-
| 100 || <code>guest</code> || Represents a common guest account anyone can login to. The password is static and known to all clients. Permissions and functionality is typically limited.
